title: Introducing commissioning aspects: case studies and equality and equity
sourceSeries: Applying a Strengths-Based Methodology to your Strategic Commissioning

lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: Our place has a highly integrated health and care system, with shared organisational leadership. We have mapped out need across the area and have a simple system of identifying five levels of need. Most of our work is structured around localities, which are engaged with the community, voluntary, and faith sectors, partly thanks to our very ambitious investment programme in that space. We have not quite got the balance of in-house and contracted provision right yet, as we still have some fairly inflexible whole-place provider contracts and some are struggling, but we are planning to bundle this differently the next time we procure, to connect better to localities.

We are experimenting in a few localities with self-organising social care and district nursing teams, and in one with dementia-friendly places. In others, where there are problems with the night-time economy, mental health, and hospital admissions, on working closely with the police, particularly at ‘hot spot’ times, we also have a key-worker service for people with very high levels of ambulance and A&E utilisation.

Ward councillors, advice services, and community groups play a role in steering locality decisions and signposting need. We are starting to engage deeply with carers and service users and have plans to bring them in to locality governance. As we had identified mental health issues and physical health as priority areas for intervention and prevention, we are working on locality-based strategies for green spaces and fitness offers, as well as seeking innovative ideas around counselling services.

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We are trying to join up locally through sharing data and planning, but outside of the formal governance structures, this does not fully carry through. There was a legal dispute between the council and clinical commissioning group about continuing healthcare funding several years ago, which resulted in some historic “bad blood” and a lack of trust. The data, at least, is useful, though we do not think it is completely accurate, as we are a ‘green and leafy’ place where we see an outflow of younger families and professionals and an inflow of retirees. Though the retirees are often relatively wealthy, increased costs of living can really bite.

We are struggling with high demand for vulnerable adult services including dementia, so that is taking up a lot of our time and attention and we are seeking more funding and to create early intervention and prevention services. We are not getting much of a response from the market on innovation and new opportunities and increased funding, even though they complained when we did a care cost and quality exercise that our focus on driving down costs was holding them back from offering us new ideas and options.

We have worked with housing associations to handle access to our limited residential care but are worried about the implications of future Care Act changes. We are beginning the journey of multi-disciplinary teams in a few locations, but there is real concern about how it will impact on social worker caseloads and time with clients, particularly as some of our clients are relatively isolated and travel times are lengthy. A major concern is the increasing number of residential care planning applications being approved, which will inevitably increase our demands and costs.

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: Whole system design is likely to highlight issues of inequality and inequity in conditions and access to services. Care should be taken to include marginalised voices in governance, leadership, and delivery, and to resist picking ‘quick wins’ which may further exclude marginalised and under-served groups.

lessons.sourceAspectHeading: Aspect 2. Relationships and organisation across the system
lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: Our relationships have taken a lot of work to get where they are today. We had a legacy among lead members and senior NHS executives of some highly volatile and difficult individuals, failed attempts to engage with and form a coalition of the voluntary and community sector, tough provider negotiations, and a tradition of commissioners who were very good technically and delivered mostly good processes, but didn’t engage much with individuals outside of the formal processes. There was a feeling that everyone was trying to pass on costs to everyone else, and trust was low.

Things started to change with a new political leadership which coincided with several senior leaders moving on. This offered an opportunity to address and reset some of the resentments that still simmered. We started to build a new outcomes-focused plan as we entered into ICS planning and held a facilitated session which encouraged us – in a safe way – to air all those old opinions about each other. Although that was not comfortable, we found it was safe, and important, to do, and set a new tone.

The real breakthrough was joint locality visits – we went jointly (social care, health, and political leaders) to engage with staff and citizens in various places, and to hear people’s experience of our care system first-hand. That was very powerful and led to things like people with experience on our decision-making boards and regular back-to-the floor and mystery shopping exercises which have helped to keep us all focused on the big picture. That does not mean there have not been some really strong disagreements, but those have more often been useful than destructive. We are really focused on broadening beyond the ICS plans to include coproduction, providers, community groups, and other parts of the council and public services who can help.

We eventually learned that all the credit we gained with providers with really good up-front engagement was lost with a very stiff and formal procurement process – which presented providers with a fait accompli after all our talk of partnering and coproduction – and then weak contract management, even when they were coming to us with innovative ideas. We are working on that now, and that involves building a much better partnership with procurement and commercial colleagues.

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We thought our relationships were good, but now I don’t think that’s true. We have a place-based plan, part of our local strategic partnership, which is based on place-based data, but while everyone comes to the partnership board meetings, we have realised that agreement in that meeting does not mean that partner services change in line with this and that people working on the ground do not know about the plan at all.

A recent resident door-knocking exercise (following on from our experience during Covid) suggested that our understanding of vulnerability and care needs in our strategic documents might not be that accurate. We created a provider forum, but that got bogged down in price discussions and attendance is really low now. We also tried to do community engagement with ward-based ‘town hall’ meetings but they became a miserable experience that officers try to get out of attending, dealing with complaints and negativity.

We have realised now that we do need to do something about this, and that commissioners are quite well-placed to have an influence, so we are working to connect – through listening to suppliers, citizen groups and frontline care workers, at first. And the Mayor has set up informal networking before the strategic partnering meetings. We know there is a lot of work to do on this!

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: Good quality relationships allow the challenging of issues to be done safely.  They need to be built for the long-term and embedded, for inequality to be challenged and overcome. Relationship-building must consciously include formerly-excluded groups, if it is to be valuable.  Commissioners and systems need to be aware of the risk that a focus on building relationships can reduce the willingness to challenge norms and problematic issues.

lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: Unlocking potential is the heart of our strategic commissioning approach. We have invested significantly in community development, shifted several large contracts over time from large commercial national providers to small local providers (leading to more money recycled in the local economy, more quickly, making a real impact on people on the edge of poverty). Adult wellness – building from our Ageing Better programme – is a core service and part of a joined-up, place-based strategy (mostly led by the council, but we’re working on it!) which links with lifelong learning, town centre generation, and access to good work to try to deal with poverty, low skills, and low productivity largely due to ill health. Our community connection activities are also linked to social prescribing and remuneration for co-production work, governance roles, and consultation.

We now routinely commission with a mix of grants, contracts, and mixed models, offering long-term funding where possible, covering overheads, seeking minimal or no bid costs where possible (this has proved much harder to do for NHS spend given the regulations). Alliance contracting has proved helpful for this. Where we do traditional contracting, we have strong social value commitments – and, more importantly, contractual commitments – to social outcomes, co-production, quality of employment, and joining our provider collaborative to look at workforce development (and recruitment and retention) as a whole place. We also have a commitment to map existing assets and delivery servicing before bringing in new contracts, and to have a market development plan which shows how each contract will leave our provider markets healthier.

All of this has been really difficult, and we could not have achieved it without staunch support from senior leaders and politicians, and without linking to their priorities for the council and place as a whole. It helped to have money to invest. Many commercial providers have also been very positive, particularly about freedom to innovate during service delivery.

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We have had to cut our grants to the voluntary sector and use social prescribing and asset-based approaches as ways of mitigating service savings, as funding has reduced and thresholds for access have increased. We are currently reviewing our information, advice, and guidance contract and hope to make cuts and award to a single provider (with sub-contractors) to be able to manage the relationship better and demonstrate better value for money. We have introduced standard social value clauses and a requirement for local investment and a proportion of local sub-contracting. We commission a lot of capability building and support services, but usually small scale and not joined up.

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: It is important to take a critical perspective regarding the impact of deprivation, exclusion, and intersectional factors on the capability of people to provide their own support, and not make assumptions about this capability. Additionally, some people who are otherwise in highly privileged groups will not necessarily be privileged (in terms, for example, of close and engaged social networks) when it comes to their ability to be supported in their home and community. At the same time, traditional service provision is likely to be biased and have built-in assumptions about needs and how they should be met, which will impact different groups in different ways. The same suspension of assumption and genuine exploration needs to apply to groups and organisations providing support, which may have very different perspectives, strengths, and weaknesses depending on their context.

lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We work hard to base all service provision on “what do you really need?” conversations with citizens. We give social workers and others who have these conversations a lot of discretion to meet needs directly, based on these conversations (within budgetary limits), and pilots show that this reduces the overall cost of care. We have expanded this to an advocacy/case management role when appropriate. A few years ago, we mapped out entire user journeys and found that our own systems being unable to hear what people were actually asking for was costing us millions in incorrect specifications with serious knock-on effects. It has been a long journey to build everyone’s trust in a focus on understanding and meeting needs opposed to formal assessment processes, and we are going through another version of that journey now as we introduce more community options and social prescribing. We have some senior politicians on board and a new DASS who is really supportive. A breakthrough moment came when we took the finance director on a site visit, and they saw that we were working on real value not on budgets – but that it was also good for budgets.

To be honest, our approach has probably slowed integration and we are still struggling to make it work in the NHS, but we have confidence we will get there. We are linking to the NHS “Getting It Right First Time” (GIRFT) programme, to try to communicate it better. We also now have enthusiastic fans amongst the user base, who are powerful advocates. We still have lots of traditional contracts and formally assessed provision – but at minimum we are including user feedback (“did you get what you needed?” and so on) as part of the evaluation criteria and building in learning and adaptation – our big lesson has been that learning is key.

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We attempted once to create a marketplace for self-funders from which we would also call off services, and a combination of technological and market challenges and leadership challenges meant that it was seen as a failure, so there is a real fear of being too ambitious in this space. We are working hard on social care and health integration and hearing a lot about avoiding ‘unwarranted variations’ in provision.

We are really pushing to move to what are called ‘outcomes-based contracts’ – in fact, our providers are leading us to some extent on that. But that is usually based on our assumptions and definitions of outcomes. We are aware that access to our services is messy and confusing, and it is hard for people to get what they really want, so we have commissioned two specialist information advice and guidance services (for dementia and carer support) as tests.

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: Equality and equity must be central to this aspect, because making assumptions about care outcomes or forcing individuals into standardised processes, services, and systems of care presents perhaps the greatest risk to a fair and equitable system. At the same time, attempts to ‘put citizens in the driving seat’ also risk a bias towards historically privileged groups and meeting or supporting the needs of those who are best able to access decision-makers and communicate in familiar and accepted ways. Therefore, co-production and advocacy must enable appropriate representation and must be done in a way and in a context that guards against these risks.

lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We’ve tried to play it clever in commissioning, since social care here used to be very traditional and siloed – we have built alliances, supported services in crisis (even when timescales meant we couldn’t really follow the process we would have liked), done mini-training for everyone in the directorate, and even ensured that we win a few awards for innovations, sharing credit with the services. We work closely with the team that used to be our Health and Care Observatory, and with the teams supporting governance at council and ICS level. We also work closely with the Finance Business Partners, who are critical to what gets approved, or not, in the annual budget.

We have run dedicated external and in-house capability-building, most of it based on action learning and pulling in mixed teams from across different council services and partners to work on real problems and build relationships. We also made co-commissioning with user and citizen voice groups part of our journey from the start, and have affinity groups, citizen commissioners, and we’re about to engage with our first Citizen Jury – this one is on the climate crisis so there’s some important overlaps, but we want to learn the process before running one on learning disabilities and transitions from children’s social care, as both are major issues in our borough.

We have also found that community groups and providers are some of our biggest allies – we recently let a home care contract in a way that both invited innovative bids and encouraged ongoing innovation in service delivery, designed by users and care staff, and we have found even some losing providers have been in touch, keen to share the model elsewhere.

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We have had a few false starts with ‘commissioning’ – on one extreme we went to a whole-council commissioning model, but there was not enough clarity about how that worked, and commissioners and providers reported to the same line managers. There also was not much recognition of how adult social care was different. Then we went to the other extreme and for a while the main team with the ‘commissioner’ job title was the team processing direct payments. We now have a team in social care with the job title ‘strategic commissioner’, but they have to go to services for most of their data, and Members and our partnership boards have expressed the opinion that ‘commissioning is over’ (it’s still associated with the ‘purchaser/provider split’). At the moment, most of their skills are around important technical areas such as the legal requirements for market shaping, but we are planning some development work and actually commissioning plays a big role in our service planning, due to some major contracts coming up where big savings are earmarked.

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: Without good information, the opportunity to innovate and change, and the skill to do so, the cause of equality and equity cannot be effectively advanced. Care must be taken not to make insights a reflection of our own prejudices.  Engaging excluded voices and welcoming active challenge is one powerful tool to guard against this. It is important to establish and stick to agreed values in this space. The inequality in power dynamics between commissioners and populations becomes starker when commissioners are more powerful and more effective, but effective commissioners can also be the most direct route towards redressing this balance. Empowering communities as commissioners empower themselves is a powerful way to address this paradox.

lessons.sourceAspectHeading: Aspect 6. Managing the policy and compliance landscape
lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We have done lots of work to make sure we really understand what we are doing regarding compliance. We built policies with the legal team, people with lived experience, and excluded groups, and we engaged with health colleagues to make sure we had a consistent approach (and necessary differences were clearly identified). We worked with policy and procurement people to shape ways of working we could reliably keep to, so that, along with all our business cases, we have a compliance case and a fuller equalities impact assessment.

It is a lot of work but because we have really worked it through, it adds value. It also makes it much harder for people to criticise our work once it has been through the whole process. We became a Social Value case study and we are talking with DHSC about adopting the new white paper guidance early, which gives us the opportunity to feed back (and is going to be quite important for our financial sustainability).

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We do occasionally run into problems with procurement telling us that our most innovative plans are not a good fit with policy, and often that has to go to the corporate management team to get resolved. We have also had a couple of challenges under the Equalities Act which caused us to reconsider some big recommissioning work.

In general, we understand the framework we have to work within, and we stick to it – this also means that when working with users and practitioners, we have the cover of the Care Act to be able to push through required changes. We had to follow the council policy on social value, which was a bit of a missed opportunity, and our approach to market shaping actually needs to be shaken up a bit – that will be an opportunity to work with providers to come up with something a bit more fit-for-purpose – just in time for the new requirements!

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: A strong policy and compliance approach to equality is very important, as is responding to compliance requirements with equality and equity in mind. It is important to recognise that compliance with regulation is not a full answer to supporting equality, diversity, and inclusion, but just the beginning.

lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: Increasingly, all our commissioning is done across partners, with providers and in co-production with people who draw on services. This means that we are putting much greater emphasis on getting a good and legally compliant process in place – but we see that as a platform to work together on ongoing learning and practice. In a recent homecare contract, we were participating in weekly sprint meetings at one stage as service patterns were developed jointly with carers and service users. We were paying close attention to the implications for cost, but it did come in within the budget envelope, and we learned a lot. We have found it useful to blend different sources of data to understand what a service can provide – from service users, practitioners, population data, things we’ve picked up from elsewhere, and so on. Extra Care housing was a major capital investment, so that side of things was a much stricter, more formal process, however we want to go back to prototyping how the service actually works once the buildings are ready to run.

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We follow the classic commissioning process. The challenge is that we never have enough time. When we can do it, we really go to town and thoroughly analyse high-quality data to identify needs, current provision, gaps, opportunities for innovation etc to come up with a ‘perfect spec’. The challenge is that, often, we just get squeezed out of time to do that properly and by the time we go to market we often find we are having to make in-year savings, so a lot of that work can feel insignificant.

Even in less-than ideal contracts with problematic providers, we often end up running the contract for an extra year to give ourselves time to run a proper OJEU process. As part of trying to stretch budget to meet needs, we are increasingly letting very long contracts to try to support lower prices and meet some of the needs of the voluntary and community sector. Because we want to start at the start and get the specification right, and because of all these challenges, we probably are not great on contract management. When we get the time, we do a thorough lessons learned exercise at contract close – part of feeding into the needs specification. Overall, I think we could be closer to practice, and we find co-production hard to get right. We have also found it hard to align our processes with those of partners, who seem to operate in very different ways.

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: A strong process needs to build in the following elements:
Understanding of unmet and marginalised need
Access for those who may be excluded
Strong equality and equity in specification and contract management
Co-design and shared learning with excluded groups

lessons.title: Case studies and Equality and equity considerations

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores higher in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We work on service design alongside strategic commissioning and have a system of ‘circles’ which connect selections of practitioners, carers, those with lived experience etc to talk about practice and share and expand on good ideas. These have enabled us to really build on earlier assistive technology work and this is becoming a major feature of some of our work. We have also identified lots of opportunities to improve joining-up and signposting between services, which has saved significant amounts from our advice contract as well as provided much earlier intervention to support citizens who would otherwise have been put off from asking for care until much later.

We have recently merged three smaller contracts, shared one across health and social care, and considered a public sector mutual for a former in-house service (though in the end the employees preferred the TUPE option). We have co-designed a new carer support service which is borough-wide and mostly provided through mutual aid. In general, we find that really understanding delivery model options and how they might affect practice on the ground is a ‘superpower’ when it comes to getting buy-in from social workers and other staff, and from politicians.

sections.heading: A case study of a council and place that scores lower in this aspect

paragraphs.text: We tend to consider delivery models only at the contractual level, and probably miss some opportunities for innovation. We did recently put out a tender for some innovation work, particularly around new technology, and we are looking forward to seeing how that goes. We recently consolidated our information, advice, and guidance contracts and saved a lot of money along with creating improved referral journeys. We have noticed that second-tier councils and housing providers are a significant part of competition for workers with our care services, so we need to work out how to address that. Most of our work with providers post-contract is monitoring and focusing on cost reduction opportunities and making sure they stick to the service provision agreed in the contract.

sections.heading: Equality and equity considerations with this aspect

paragraphs.text: It is with practice on the ground, enabled by delivery models, that equality and equity are either supported or fail. It is important to think about the implications of changes in delivery models, particularly innovative ones and those using novel technology (or with digital access) for those who are traditionally marginalised and excluded, and groups who could be marginalised or excluded by the new model.
